content.text:
I accepted the challenge in full and saved the revised finding as `finding.json`. I ran no new queries: every number cites either my earlier queries or the challenger's, and I found nothing in theirs to dispute.

**What changed:**
- **The material effect is about a third of what I claimed.** Jobs whose material arrived after the purchase order's due date were usually the tightly planned ones: 0.5129 of them had 14 days or less of planned slack, against 0.1766 of other jobs (q367). Planned slack here is the gap between the purchase order's due date and the date promised to the customer. Comparing jobs with the same year and the same slack, late-material jobs shipped late 0.3573 of the time against 0.1263. That is 2.83 times as often, not about nine, and comes to about 81.4 extra late shipments a year, not 111.9 (q366).
- **The two lateness spikes have different causes.**
  - **2016:** jobs were released with normal slack, but ran late more often at every slack level. That points to a delay inside the plant after release (q360, q362).
  - **2021:** vendor lead times roughly doubled (q357). A job can't be released until its last material arrives (q352), so jobs were released with less slack. That explains about 0.394 of the 2021 excess. The other 0.606 is higher lateness at the same slack, like 2016 (q362, q367). That split depends on the order the decomposition is done in. The late-material flag missed this because "on time" was measured against due dates that had themselves been pushed out.
- **I dropped the "work flowed more slowly" evidence.** Time from release to completion fell steadily over the decade, and 2017 matched 2021 on it with few late shipments (q344).
- **One narrowing of my own:** using the challenger's q344, every late shipment in every year was on a job finished after its promise date. So the delay happened before completion, not between completion and shipping.
- **New limits stated:** receipts go unrecorded unevenly by vendor, and the two outside processors record none at all, so their timeliness can't be measured (q338, q341). Data before early 2016 is incomplete (q335, q336).

I lowered confidence from high to medium, because one added control moved the size of the material effect threefold. There is still no dollar figure. The finding still can't say which work centre held jobs in the spikes, because operations record only completion dates.
